newsitem.title: BELGIUM: HENEX ANOTHER UNDERVALUED BELGIAN HOLDING.
newsitem.headline: HENEX ANOTHER UNDERVALUED BELGIAN HOLDING.

text.p: Belgian brokerage and stock pickers Cels Guigon Securities BV said on Wednesday shares in Belgian holding company Henex -- part of the Boel family- controlled Boel Group -- were undervalued and should be bought.
Henex was trading at too large a discount to its intrinsic value as were two of its main interests -- holding company Sofina and steel firm Fafer .
Henex was at 76,000 francs on Wednesday's Brussels bourse, unchanged from Tuesday's close which was also its 1997 high.
The share underperformed the Bel-20 index in recent months, but pounded ahead in the past week, rallying from 67,500.

Cels said Henex should benefit from an expected improvement in steel prices and volumes at Fafer. Noting a comparatively close correlation between the share prices of Fafer and Hoogovens of the Netherlands, it said that relative to its intrinsic value Fafer was undervalued by some 30 percent.

Since the start of the year Hoogovens has risen by some 46 percent; Fafer has been more volatile, starting the year at 71,000 francs, peaking at 115,750 francs in March and currently trading at 107,900 francs.
Dutch steel major Hoogovens recently concluded a cooperation deal with a member of the Boel Group, its Usines Gustave Boel, a Belgian steel maker.
Cels said speculation Hoogovens might buy Fafer was another reason to buy Henex stock.
Henex owns over 22 percent in Fafer, while Fafer has 4.5 percent of Henex. Henex was split off from Fafer in 1981.
Cels said Sofina, which holds 3.8 percent in Belgian insurer Royale Belge and has shares in oil group PetroFina and retailer GIB , was undervalued by some 23 percent relative to its intrinsic value.

Generale Bank said earlier on Wednesday it upgraded shares in GIB to speculative 'hold' from 'sell'. It expected GIB to take "concrete (and maybe energetic) measures to eventually put net current results in line with sales in the coming months."

Cels noted that vis a vis other Belgian holding companies such as GBL and Brederode the Henex share had been lagging. Since the start of the year GBL stock has gained 47 percent, while Brederode is up 44 percent.
Holding company stock has been in the limelight since various chief executive officers said the discount of their shares to the underlying values was too large.
One company to act on that view has been Almanij, which last month moved to split up the assets of holding company Gevaert between itself and holding company Cobepa .

The move has focused attention on Almanij, whose star holding is Belgium's third largest bank Kredietbank . Analysts now see Almanij a promisng play in a possible reshaping of Belgium's overcrowded banking scene.
